sheets.rejected_alternative: Standalone .claude/ configuration copied into each repository. It works for one project, but there is no version, no update channel and no single place to fix a bug, so 40 copies drift apart the first time the review helper changes.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns loading, namespacing and version resolution, and managed settings can force-enable the plugin so a repo cannot silently drop it. The model owns whether the skills actually get used once loaded; the hooks inside the plugin are the harness-owned part of the bundle.
sheets.context_boundary: Everything loads into whichever session enables the plugin: skill descriptions and subagent definitions occupy main-session context, MCP tool names load at startup with schemas on demand, and hooks cost nothing until they return output. Nothing crosses between the 40 consuming repos; the plugin is the shared artifact, not shared state.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies from the moment the plugin is enabled in a repo and reloads on /reload-plugins within a session. Updates reach consumers when the marketplace entry moves and the consumer updates: with an explicit version, only a bump ships an update; without one, a git-distributed plugin treats every commit as a new version. It stops applying on disable or uninstall, or when a --plugin-dir local copy shadows it for a session.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory at the distribution layer unless you force it. Repos that never run the update, or that pin an old marketplace commit, quietly keep the old helper, so 'reaches every consumer' is only true if managed settings force-enable the plugin or strictPluginOnlyCustomization is set. Structural mistakes are the other common failure: putting skills/, hooks/ or agents/ inside .claude-plugin/ instead of at the plugin root makes components silently not load, and a same-named project or user agent overrides the plugin's.
sheets.version_caveat: No plan gate for authoring or private distribution. Version behaviour hinges on the optional version field (omit it and every commit SHA counts as a new version). Keeping the marketplace in a private repository is the supported way to stay internal; the public community marketplace requires review and, for the claude.ai submission form, a Team or Enterprise org. Managed-settings levers (enabledPlugins force-enable, allowManagedHooksOnly, strictPluginOnlyCustomization) are read only from managed settings, and --plugin-dir cannot override a plugin that managed settings force-enable or force-disable.

sheets.primary: One plugin that bundles the review skill, the lifecycle hooks, and the tracker MCP server behind a single .claude-plugin/plugin.json manifest, published through a marketplace hosted in a private repo the platform team controls. Consumer repos enable it via enabledPlugins at project scope, or the org force-enables it in managed settings, and releases are cut by bumping the manifest version.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Standalone .claude/ configuration copied into each repository. It loses at 40 consumers: there is no version identity, no update channel, and no way to ship a fix without 40 pull requests, and skill names collide across sources instead of being namespaced.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code resolves the marketplace, installs the plugin, and loads its skills, hooks, and MCP servers from the enabledPlugins entry without the model participating. The one model-owned residue is whether the bundled skill actually gets invoked once loaded.
sheets.context_boundary: Each consumer session loads the plugin into its own context: the skill contributes a listing entry there, the MCP server contributes tool schemas, and the hooks run as separate processes outside any context window. Nothing crosses between consumer repos; the plugin ships code and text, not shared state.
sheets.lifecycle: Installed once per consumer (or force-enabled by policy), then re-resolved on update when the computed version differs from the cached copy. It stops applying when the plugin is uninstalled or its enabledPlugins entry is set false; that user setting persists across updates and reinstalls.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and quietly on the distribution axis. With an explicit version in plugin.json, pushing commits without bumping the field ships nothing and /plugin update reports the consumer is already current, so 40 repos silently sit on a stale review helper. Conversely, omitting version means every commit is an update, so an accidental push reaches all consumers. A plugin that updates mid-session also leaves hooks and MCP servers on the old path until /reload-plugins or a restart.
sheets.version_caveat: No CLI version floor for plugins themselves, but the org-wide guarantees are managed-settings-only keys: strictPluginOnlyCustomization to force all skills, agents, hooks, and MCP servers to come from plugins, strictKnownMarketplaces and blockedMarketplaces to restrict sources, and disableSideloadFlags (Claude Code v2.1.193 or later) to stop per-run bypasses via --plugin-dir. Community-marketplace submission through the claude.ai form additionally requires a Team or Enterprise organization.

scenarios.scenario: A production bug has five plausible root causes. We want five investigators working simultaneously, each defending one hypothesis and actively trying to disprove the others' findings through direct back-and-forth, converging on a written consensus.

key.primary: An agent team: enable CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1, then have the lead spawn five teammates who share the task list and message each other directly over the mailbox system
key.rejected_alternative: Spawning five parallel subagents from the main session, one per hypothesis
key.rejection_reason: The agent-teams doc's comparison table is decisive: subagents 'report results back to the main agent only' and 'never talk to each other,' while teammates 'message each other directly' and self-coordinate on a shared task list. The requirement is peer-to-peer challenge, which subagents structurally cannot do; the docs even use competing-hypotheses debugging as the canonical team example.
key.enforcement_owner: split: the harness supplies the machinery subagents structurally lack, direct teammate mailboxes and the shared task list; the model owns actually conducting the adversarial debate and converging on the written consensus
key.lifecycle: Gated behind the CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 env var or settings entry; team forms when the lead spawns the first teammate with user approval; cleanup on session end
key.failure_mode: Fails closed at spawn: without CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 no team is set up, no team directories are written, and Claude does not spawn or propose teammates; a running team fails soft: task status can lag when a teammate fails to mark work complete, blocking dependent tasks, and /resume or /rewind does not restore in-process teammates, so the lead may message teammates that no longer exist; two investigators editing the same findings file overwrite each other.
key.version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default; requires CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1. Behavior described as of v2.1.178 (TeamCreate/TeamDelete removed); known limitations include no /resume of in-process teammates and one team per session

sheets.primary: An Agent Team: one lead session plus five teammates, each assigned one hypothesis, sharing a task list and messaging each other directly, with the lead synthesising the written consensus. Enabled by setting `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1`.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Five subagents fanned out from one session. Subagents only report results back to the caller and never talk to each other, so the required direct back-and-forth between investigators cannot happen; the lead would have to relay every exchange.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model, and diffusely: nobody owns coordination centrally. Each teammate is an independent Claude instance deciding what to claim and what to challenge, while the harness supplies only the shared task list, the messaging and the lifecycle.
sheets.context_boundary: Six independent context windows, one per participant. What crosses between them is only the messages teammates send each other and the shared task list; one investigator's findings do not appear in a peer's window unless that peer is messaged, and the consensus write-up is a separate artifact the lead produces.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts when the lead spawns teammates in a session that has the environment variable set; teammates run until their tasks are done or the lead stops them, and cleanup happens automatically at session exit. One team per session, no nesting, and the lead is fixed for the session's lifetime.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails by stalling rather than erroring: a teammate can hold an assigned task and go quiet, shutdown waits for in-flight tool calls, and `/resume` and `/rewind` do not restore in-process teammates, leaving a resumed lead messaging peers that no longer exist. Cost is the second failure, since each teammate is a separate Claude instance and five of them multiply token spend.
sheets.version_caveat: Experimental and off by default: it requires `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` in settings or the environment, and without it no team is set up at all. The no-setup-step and auto-cleanup behaviour described is as of v2.1.178, where `TeamCreate` and `TeamDelete` no longer exist, and `--teammate-mode` is itself experimental and absent from `claude --help`.

sheets.primary: An agent team: the main session becomes the lead and spawns five named teammates, one per hypothesis, instructed to message each other directly and try to disprove the others' theories, with the surviving consensus written to a findings document. The shared task list and direct teammate messaging are what make the adversarial round trips possible.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Five subagents spawned through the Agent tool. It loses on the one mechanism the scenario names: subagents report only back to the caller and cannot talk to each other, so any cross-examination would have to be relayed turn by turn through the lead's context, which serialises the debate and re-introduces the anchoring the design is meant to avoid.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead agent decides who to spawn, what each defends, when the debate has converged, and what the written consensus says; the harness only provides the messaging transport, the shared task list, and the permission checks on each teammate's tool calls.
sheets.context_boundary: Five separate context windows plus the lead's. Each teammate loads the project's CLAUDE.md, MCP servers, and skills afresh and receives only its spawn prompt; the lead's conversation history does not carry over. What crosses the boundary is the spawn prompt going out, inter-teammate messages, task status, idle notifications, and the final synthesis returning to the lead.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts when the lead spawns teammates in response to the request, runs while teammates hold the debate, and ends when they go idle and the lead synthesises. Cleanup is automatic on session exit; teammates do not survive the session, and /resume does not restore in-process ones.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory throughout, and it degrades quietly. Teammates sometimes fail to mark tasks complete, which blocks dependent work and makes a run look hung; shutdown is slow because each finishes its current tool call; and after a resume the lead may message teammates that no longer exist. There is nothing forcing genuine adversarial review, so five agents can converge politely on the first plausible cause, and the token cost is roughly five sessions rather than one.
sheets.version_caveat: Agent teams are experimental and off by default: CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 must be set in settings.json or the environment, and without it Claude will not spawn or even propose teammates. The behaviour described here is as of v2.1.178, where the separate TeamCreate and TeamDelete setup step was removed; teammate display mode defaults to in-process from v2.1.179, and split panes need tmux or iTerm2.

sheets.primary: An agent team: the session becomes the lead and spawns five teammates, one per hypothesis, instructed to message each other directly and try to disprove each other's theories, with the shared task list coordinating and a findings document as the written deliverable. This is the documented use case for debugging with competing hypotheses, and the adversarial debate is the mechanism, since it is what defeats the anchoring a single investigator falls into.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Subagents. They parallelise just as well, but they can only report back to the main agent and never talk to each other, so there is no direct back-and-forth and the lead would have to relay every challenge, which reintroduces the single point of anchoring.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness provides the mailboxes, the task list with file-locked claiming, and the spawn mechanics, but which hypothesis survives, when the debate is over, and what the consensus says are all model judgements. Hooks (TeammateIdle, TaskCompleted) are the only place to put a harness-owned gate on that.
sheets.context_boundary: Six context windows: the lead's plus one per teammate, each fully independent. Each teammate loads project CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills itself but does not inherit the lead's conversation history, so the spawn prompt must carry the bug details. What crosses between them is SendMessage traffic through the JSON mailboxes, the shared task list, and files written to disk, which is why the consensus should land in a document rather than only in someone's window.
sheets.lifecycle: The team forms when the first teammate spawns and is scoped to that session; the lead is fixed for the session's lifetime and teammates cannot spawn their own. It ends when teammates are asked to shut down or the session exits, at which point the team config directory is cleaned up automatically while the task list persists under cleanupPeriodDays retention.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory, expensive, and prone to stalling. Token cost scales linearly with five separate Claude instances; teammates sometimes stop on errors rather than recovering, task status lags so dependent work blocks, and the lead may declare the investigation finished before the debate has converged (tell it to wait). Two teammates editing the same findings file overwrite each other, so give the write to one owner. Nothing in the mechanism guarantees the surviving theory is correct; it is a bias-reduction pattern, not a proof.
sheets.version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default: nothing happens without CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 in settings.json or the environment. The no-setup-step spawn and automatic cleanup describe v2.1.178 and later (TeamCreate and TeamDelete no longer exist, and team_name is accepted but ignored). Known limits: /resume and /rewind do not restore in-process teammates, one team per session, no nested teams, and split panes need tmux or iTerm2 with it2, which rules them out in VS Code's terminal, Windows Terminal and Ghostty.

sheets.primary: An agent team, with five teammates each assigned one hypothesis and able to message each other directly, converging on a written consensus document. The distinguishing requirement is the direct back-and-forth: peer-to-peer challenge is what separates a team from a fan-out.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Five parallel subagents dispatched from one orchestrator, rejected because subagents cannot talk to one another, they only report back to the parent, so cross-examination would have to be relayed by the orchestrator and the adversarial pressure is lost.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The orchestration, the assignment of hypotheses and the quality of the disconfirmation are all model behaviour; nothing in the harness verifies that anyone genuinely tried to falsify anyone else.
sheets.context_boundary: Each teammate has its own context window and does its own investigation there. Inter-agent messages and the final written artefact cross boundaries; the raw investigation transcripts do not, so the lead sees summaries and the consensus document rather than five full histories.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts when the team is spawned for this specific bug and ends when the consensus document is written or the run is stopped. It is a one-shot investigation structure, not standing configuration, so it does not apply to the next bug unless spawned again.
sheets.failure_mode: Expensive and advisory. The characteristic failures are premature convergence on whichever hypothesis is argued most fluently, five agents rediscovering the same log line, and an agent defending its assigned hypothesis past the point where evidence killed it because it was told to defend it. Require each teammate to state the evidence that would disconfirm its own hypothesis, and have a separate reviewer check the consensus against the actual artefacts.
sheets.version_caveat: Agent teams with inter-agent messaging are among the newest and least settled mechanisms and may still be experimental or behind an enabling flag or setting; I do not know the flag name or the version gate, so confirm the capability exists on the installed build before designing around direct agent-to-agent communication rather than orchestrator relay.

scenarios.scenario: Our path-based blocks stop the agent's own file tools from reading ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh, but a Python script it launches can still open those files directly. We need every process the agent spawns, including children of children, to be physically unable to read those paths.

key.primary: Enable the Bash sandbox (sandbox.enabled) with sandbox.credentials file entries or sandbox.filesystem.denyRead for the credential paths; Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap on Linux/WSL2 enforce the boundary on the process tree
key.rejected_alternative: Read deny rules such as Read(~/.aws/credentials) and Read(~/.ssh/**) in permissions settings
key.rejection_reason: The permissions docs warn that Read and Edit deny rules apply to Claude's built-in file tools and to file commands Claude Code recognizes in Bash, like cat, head, tail, and sed, but not to arbitrary subprocesses that open files themselves, and they point to enabling the sandbox for OS-level enforcement that blocks all processes from accessing a path.
key.context_boundary: no context window (the boundary is an OS-level sandbox enforced at command execution time, blocking all processes rather than just Claude's own tools); the protected credential contents never reach any context, and the boundary holds even when a prompt injection has already steered Claude's decisions
key.lifecycle: OS-level boundary applied to every sandboxed Bash command and all child processes at execution time; subagents inherit the parent session's sandbox configuration
key.failure_mode: No native Windows support; the sandbox's default read policy still permits credential files until you explicitly deny them; and unless allowUnsandboxedCommands is set to false, the dangerouslyDisableSandbox escape hatch can rerun a failing command outside the boundary.
key.version_caveat: Sandbox runs on macOS, Linux, and WSL2 only (not native Windows); the sandbox.credentials block requires v2.1.187 or later

sheets.primary: Enable sandboxing: sandbox.enabled true with sandbox.filesystem.denyRead listing ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh, or the equivalent sandbox.credentials.files entries with mode "deny". This is OS-level isolation (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap plus seccomp on Linux and WSL2) that applies to the Bash tool and every process descended from it, which is exactly the layer path-based permission rules do not reach.
sheets.rejected_alternative: More Read(...) deny rules, or a PreToolUse hook that scans Bash commands for those paths. Both operate on what Claude Code itself can see and inspect, and neither can stop a Python interpreter that has already been launched from calling open() on the file.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness sets the boundary and the OS kernel enforces it. Once the sandbox is up, nothing the model decides and nothing a spawned process does can reopen the path.
sheets.context_boundary: Enforcement happens at the process boundary of the sandboxed Bash command, outside every context window. What reaches the model's context is only the resulting permission-denied error in the command's stderr, which it can read and react to but not route around.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies to each sandboxed Bash invocation from session start onward. Commands listed in sandbox.excludedCommands and calls that pass dangerouslyDisableSandbox run outside the boundary, so set allowUnsandboxedCommands to false to close that escape hatch, and keep excludedCommands minimal.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open by default in the one case that matters most: if the sandbox cannot start because bwrap or socat is missing or the platform is unsupported, Claude Code prints a warning and runs commands unsandboxed. Set failIfUnavailable true to make it a hard startup gate. It also covers only Bash and its children, so the model's own in-process Read tool still needs the matching Read deny rule; the two sets are merged into the final boundary.
sheets.version_caveat: Sandboxing is macOS, Linux and WSL2 only, so a native Windows fleet gets no coverage from this mechanism at all. sandbox.credentials.files and credentials.envVars require v2.1.187 or later, filesystem.disabled requires v2.1.216, network.strictAllowlist requires v2.1.219, and filesystem.allowManagedReadPathsOnly is managed-settings-only (it locks allowRead to managed entries while denyRead still merges from every source).

sheets.primary: Claude Code's OS-level Bash sandbox, enabled in managed settings: sandbox.enabled true with sandbox.filesystem.denyRead listing ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh (or the equivalent sandbox.credentials.files entries), plus sandbox.failIfUnavailable true and sandbox.allowUnsandboxedCommands false so there is no escape hatch.
sheets.rejected_alternative: More Read and Edit deny rules, or a PreToolUse hook on Bash that inspects the command. Both act at the tool-call boundary and are blind to a file that an already-running Python interpreter opens itself, which is precisely the gap described.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, delegating to the OS kernel: sandbox-exec on macOS and bubblewrap plus a seccomp filter on Linux and WSL2. The boundary is enforced on the process, not on the model's intent, so a prompt injection cannot talk its way past it.
sheets.context_boundary: There is no context-window boundary here; the boundary is the sandboxed process tree. The command and every descendant run inside it and get an ordinary permission error on the denied path, which returns as normal tool output.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies to every Bash command Claude Code runs and to their child processes, for the life of the session. It stops applying for anything listed in sandbox.excludedCommands and for any call made with the dangerouslyDisableSandbox parameter unless allowUnsandboxedCommands is set to false.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed at the kernel once it is up, but fails open at startup by default: if the sandbox cannot start because of an unsupported platform or a missing bwrap or socat binary, Claude Code prints a warning and runs commands unsandboxed, which is why failIfUnavailable must be set for a hard gate. excludedCommands and dangerouslyDisableSandbox are the two deliberate holes.
sheets.version_caveat: Bash sandboxing is macOS, Linux, and WSL2 only and defaults to false, so a Windows-native fleet gets no coverage from it; the mirror's sandboxing page is absent, so that Windows conclusion rests on the platform list in the settings table rather than on a direct statement. sandbox.credentials.files requires v2.1.187 or later, filesystem.disabled v2.1.216, and network.strictAllowlist v2.1.219.

sheets.primary: Turn on the OS level bash sandbox through managed settings: sandbox.enabled true, with ~/.aws/credentials and ~/.ssh in sandbox.filesystem.denyRead (or as sandbox.credentials.files deny entries), allowUnsandboxedCommands false and failIfUnavailable true.
sheets.rejected_alternative: More Read deny permission rules, which is the control already in place. They cover Claude's own file tools and the file commands Claude Code recognizes inside Bash, but they are a tool level check, not a process level one, so a spawned interpreter is unaffected.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness delegating to the operating system. Claude Code launches Bash inside the platform sandbox, and the boundary binds all subprocess commands rather than just Claude's file tools.
sheets.context_boundary: Enforcement sits at the process boundary, not the context window. The sandboxed command and its descendants get a permission denied from the OS, and only that error text reaches the model.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies to every sandboxed Bash command and its child processes from the moment the settings are read at startup, for the whole session. It stops applying to anything listed in excludedCommands, and to any call that uses the dangerouslyDisableSandbox escape hatch while that is still permitted.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open by default when the sandbox cannot start: a warning is printed and commands run unsandboxed, so failIfUnavailable true is required to make it a hard gate. excludedCommands and dangerouslyDisableSandbox are the other two holes, which is why allowUnsandboxedCommands false belongs in the same policy.
sheets.version_caveat: Bash sandboxing is macOS, Linux and WSL2 only and defaults to false, so a native Windows shell gets no OS level enforcement at all and needs a different containment story. The sandbox.credentials.files form of the read block requires Claude Code v2.1.187 or later.

sheets.primary: OS-level isolation rather than any in-agent mechanism: run the agent inside a container or VM (a devcontainer image, or the CLI's sandboxed execution mode where the platform supports it) in which ~/.aws and ~/.ssh are simply not mounted or are removed from the namespace, so every descendant process gets a kernel-level refusal.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook that greps Bash commands for the sensitive paths; it inspects only the command the agent types, and the scenario is precisely a child process opening the file at runtime, which no command-string inspection can see.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness / operating system. Neither the model nor Claude Code's permission layer is in the enforcement path once a child process is running.
sheets.context_boundary: Enforcement is entirely below the agent: no policy text enters the model context, and what crosses back is only an ordinary permission-denied error in the tool output, which the model must be able to interpret without looping.
sheets.lifecycle: Applies for the lifetime of the container or sandboxed process tree, covering children and grandchildren automatically, and lapses the moment someone runs the agent outside the container or mounts the host home directory in.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed, which is the point, but it breaks legitimate work: git over SSH, an AWS-authenticated test, or a deploy script all start failing, and the agent can burn turns retrying and inventing workarounds unless told what is unavailable. If credentials are needed at all, the fix is short-lived scoped credentials injected as env vars, not remounting the files.
sheets.version_caveat: Claude Code has gained some built-in sandboxing for command execution, but its availability and mechanism are platform-specific (a seatbelt-style profile on macOS, a namespace/bubblewrap approach on Linux, with Windows the weakest case) and I cannot confirm the current flag name, setting key, or minimum version from memory. Treat container isolation as the portable answer and verify any built-in sandbox flag against the installed build.
